Someone asked why wouldn't Asia just take more West African (WAF) crudes and let the Saudi grades get absorbed by Europe if the big rerouting via Suez Canal happens?

It all boils down to quality. Asia can take some WAF as displacement for the Middle East crudes, but because of the high nitrogen and high TAN of the WAF grades, the refinery hits a limit fast.

That's why we didn't see WAF getting wolfed up by Korea or Japan throughout the crisis. If China is not there to buy WAF, it becomes distressed.

quotedTweet.text:
Quality of crude oil - it's not just sulphur and API

1⃣Most traders use sulphur and API to classify crude types but from a refinery point of view, this grossly oversimplifies the way the crude is evaluated for fit for use in their configuration.

2⃣Some very important qualities often overlooked by traders are the nitrogen, total acid number (TAN) and metals content. Nitrogen, vanadium and nickel content affect catalyst activity; while pipeline metallurgy has to cater for a higher TAN (i.e. carbon steel pipelines may corrode quickly if exposed to a higher TAN crude).

3⃣Middle Eastern crude which is what most Asian refineries are designed for, generally have lower nitrogen, TAN and metals content than LATAM, WAF and Canadian alternatives.

4⃣Additionally, some of these Middle Eastern crudes have superior quality for making baseoil and bitumen. Oman has elevated TAN and poor bitumen qualities compared to Upper Zakum.

5⃣This could explain why some refineries are reportedly willing to pay up for Upper Zakum at OSP+20$/bbl instead of taking Brent-linked alternatives.

#oott

text: @Fireleap_  this is for you

For those not familiar with the logistics surrounding the alternative routes for Saudi crude if the Bab el-Mandeb Strait becomes shut <editted>:  

1⃣ You normally load VLCCs (Very Large Crude Carriers) which take 2 mb of crude from Yanbu currently and Ras Tanura when Strait of Hormuz is open.   

2⃣ These VLCCs are typically the most cost economic way to freight Middle Eastern crude into Asia.  

3⃣ If the VLCC cannot transit Bab el-Mandeb strait, then it has to go north up the Red Sea and go to Ain Sukhna port, discharge part of the 2 mb cargo into the Sumed pipeline and transit via the Suez Canal at a lighter draft, to then reload the balance cargo from Sidi Kerir. Then this VLCC goes a biggggggg round from the Mediterranean Sea, make a bigggggg detour round the Cape of Good Hope to go into Asia. This extra step takes about 30 days and a lot more handling cost. <Use Google Maps to visualize what I just said>

4⃣Another way is to load the crude at Yanbu with Suezmaxes which can take 1 mb of cargo only. Use this Suezmax to transit via the Suez Canal and do that whole rerouting using the Med Sea and Cape of Good Hope. Chartering Suezmax to load 2 mb of cargo generally economically unfavourable compared to the VLCC option, but the new VLCC option is really quite bad as well.  

5⃣If your cargo HAS loaded already on a VLCC, you would need to use the Sumed pipeline way, or split the cargo into 2 Suezmax to utilize the Suez Canal way.  

All the above is $$$$$ and extra time (not to mention vessel losses also).  

#oott

Asking for help from the shipping community: 

Is the Suez Canal truly bidirectional? I.e. can we see VLCCs on ballast coming from Med into the Red Sea to load Yanbu cargoes if the Bab el Mandeb Strait is closed? #oott

For those who reposted this post, please note my latest update on point 3. You don't need a new VLCC to do the second leg. The same VLCC with a lighter draft goes into Suez Canal and reloads at Sidi Kerir. Very sorry for the misinformation

Hi folks, sorry I made an error with my point 3. The VLCC that unloads some cargo to the SUMED pipeline can then travel through the Suez Canal at a lighter draft, and reload the discharged oil at Sidi Kerir on the Med side. So you don't need to charter a whole new VLCC for the second leg of the voyage.

Thanks for all who pointed out the mistake.

The question imho isn't whether or not Trump *can* TACO on Iran—when push comes to shove I think Trump can still choose to hard-bail and leave everyone else with the mess, what I would have called the "unilateral TACO" a few months ago.

Question is at what level of market stress—crude/pump price, equity market rout, etc.—will force Trump to do so?

I always thought that the now-dead MOU read a lot like the deal I expected Trump to be forced to make at $150+ crude, and it was strange to me that Trump agreed to it at like $80. 

But clearly Trump never intended to comply with the key provisions that got Tehran to agree to reopen the Strait, which makes a lot more sense at $80. Hence why the deal—which was fundamentally unstable given competing interpretations of those key provisions—collapsed and we're back to a tightening oil market and a rising price trajectory in an attempt to find the TACO clearing price.

There's also always a possibility that Iran eventually taps out first, but I think so far Tehran seems intent on leveraging the Hormuz crisis while they're got it.

The month-long post-MOU partial reopening kind of helped give the market a temporary supply hit, but most of that was just the transfer of stranded oil-on-water in the Gulf into the broader system. Fresh Gulf loadings, meanwhile, failed to durably rebound and are falling again.

Meanwhile global commercial stock levels have continued to draw, SPRs are lower, and now we have a deepening refined product crisis on top of Hormuz thanks to Russia's Ukraine-assisted refinery fleet implosion.

So oil market is now caught between more durably tighter balances and not wanting to get rugged on the upside in an inevitable replay of prior TACO jawbones/head fakes. 

Finally, there's still that pesky presumed surplus on the other side of this crisis, which makes it easier all else equal to tolerate low stock levels (we can just refill them in the glut! right?!). But future barrels won't matter if we *actually* start getting close to local tank bottoms, which would force prices sharply higher to balance as patience is exhausted.

It's a race!

Fascinating market, hard to believe I'll ever see another one like it.

Gold sentiment is at the lows.

CTA gold positioning is lower than in 2024, even though gold is up ~60% over the same timeframe.

Why? Fear of rate hikes.

But the gold bull thesis was never about rate cuts or hikes.

It was always about:

- Endless deficits
- Unsustainable debt growth
- Dedollarization

And the war has accelerated those trends... not reversed them.

Yes, a potential rate hike would hurt gold in the short term.

But with record debt levels and trillions needing to be refinanced at much higher yields, keeping rates higher for longer becomes increasingly difficult.

The same tool used to fight inflation now risks destabilizing the funding mechanism of the government.

When forced to choose between:

1. Protecting the currency by hiking rates
2. Protecting the debt market by lowering rates

The Fed will choose the second option all day
